As you learn about the different techniques available with your machine, create your own reference cards to easily remember the carriage settings.

At first glance, any knitting machine seems complicated. Think about the dashboard in a car. There are lots of dials and buttons and levers, but once you learn the names of things you'll quickly discover what you need to make the car go.
Examine the hotspots below and learn the names of the elements that make up your knitting machine. As you work through this course, these terms will be come second-nature and you will associate the terms with the functions of the machine.

Before you start to set up your machine, identify the tools and accessories that came with your machine.
If you don't have the tools marked "essential" you'll be able to get started knitting, but ask Mr. Google to help you find them.
When looking for tools and fun accessories, keep in mind that this is a Singer/Silver/Studio 4.5mm (standard) machine.
Essential:
  • Table Clamps
  • Needle Pusher
  • Latch Tool
  • Transfer Tools
  • Claw weights
  • Oil (sewing machine oil works great)
Consider Locating:
  • Punchcards and snaps - must have for automatic patterning.
    If you don't have the original punchcards, digital copies are included in this course and you can punch your own.
  • Carriage lock - good for securing the carriage when packing it
  • Ravel Cord - "must have" for certain techniques
  • Magic Cams - required for the Single Motif technique
  • Extra needles - Nice to have on hand - you won't break needles often, but ...
  • If you plan to use the Knit Contour, you will need the pattern cards (or blanks to draw your own), the Scale Set and the Auxiliary Feeding Cam

The 4.5 mm gauge of this machine is perfect for lightweight yarns. The only limit is the size of the needles. If the yarn is too thick and doesn't fit in the hooks of the needles, it can split and/or jam the machine.

Take a moment to get familiar with the terminology and location of items on the carriage

Don't be overwhelmed by all the buttons, dials and levers on the carriage. As we cover the various techniques available, we will walk through each setting and explore it's impact on your knitting.
Instead of forming each stitch one-at-a-time like in hand knitting, the carriage acts as your hands and fingers.
  • Using the butts of the needle and the channels underneath the carriage, select which needles will knit.

  • The Tension dial controls how the yarn is fed and how large the stitches will be.

  • The Side Levers Tells the machine that you want to knit in pattern

  • The Cam Lever instruct the machine about what type of stitch pattern you want to create

  • The punchcard along with the Memory Drums automatically select needles
As you continue on your journey to master your machine, all of the other settings will become second nature to you.
Mouse over the spots to see the names of the buttons and levers
To create stitch patterns:
  1. Cam Lever
  2. Side Levers
  3. Russel Levers
  4. Needle Positions (punchcard

Memory Wheel

This is the heart of automatic patterning on a Silver/Singer/Studio punchcard machine. As the carriage passes the punchcard mechanism, the Memory Wheels record the position of the holes in the card. On the return pass of the carriage, the appropriate needles are selected and positioned according to the Cam Setting (stitch technique).
NOTE: Often on machines that have been stored for a long time the memory wheels can be locked up. The wheel should turn freely for stitch patterning to occur.

Understanding how to set your carriage for PLAIN KNITTING is essential
It is a good habit to always check your carriage settings before starting a new technique or a new piece of knitting. It's easy to have your carriage set for patterning, then come back days later and be surprised that the machine isn't knitting as expected.
Every time you sit down to knit, take time to double check the settings.

Cam Lever
Russel Lever(s)
Side Lever
Tuck Knob(s)
Weaving Knob(s)
Yarn Feeder

Save your back, neck and shoulders
In the videos in this course, you'll see me pushing the carriage with one hand. BAD!!!! I'm reaching around the camera.
When you are knitting use both hands and push and pull alternately to move the carriage.
Many knitters also adjust their knitting table so they can stand while knitting.

Arm, hand and wrist position

STOP! LOOK AT THE POSITION OF YOUR HAND AND WRIST IN RELATION TO YOUR ELBOW.Many knitters will find their elbow is below the level of the wrist and hand.
Knitting in this position, after a time, will create an ache and pain through the neck and across the shoulders. Try sitting higher so that your elbow is slightly above the wrist and hand.

More tips

  • A stool for your feet may be needed or your machine table or stand may have to be lowered.

  • If you have a stand to use your machine, the same elbow position is needed. (elbows slightly above the hands)

  • Try standing to knit. Use an adjustable table to keep the elbow position correct. Here's what I use

  • Good lighting is a must

  • A clean (and oiled) machine bed and carriage are essential.

components.html:
No matter what cast on method you use, it's important to secure the yarn tail when casting on so the first few stitches knit correctly.
Use the arrows to navigate

slides.caption:
Some knitters will tie the yarn tail to the table clamp.

You have to remember to remove this as you knit

The manual suggests securing the tail to the cast on comb

Some cast on combs don't have clips and this can be fiddly.

Use a chip clip to not only secure the tail, but it adds a little weight as well.
It's easily removed as you knit.
This method can be used any time you have a yarn tail (knitting stripes).
A spring-type clothes pin works great too!

components.html:
Whether aligned by the punchcard or manually positioned, the needle position along with the carriage settings create stitch patterns.
Vintage machine knitting patterns and instructions will refer often to these positions with abbreviations
A Non-working position  (NWP)  Unused needles
B  Working Position (WP)  Needles lined up to knit in stockinette and most pattern work
C  Middle Position (MP)  Bring the needles from holding position into working and pattern work positions
D  Holding Position (HP/Hold)  The farthest position from "A" on the needlebed

For many more cast-on tips and techniques, visit:
the Knit it Now Classroom: Cast on Methods

Open Cast on
By definition, an open cast on will have stitches that will unravel if given the chance.
Some machine manuals will give instruction for this type of cast on
The Cast on demonstrated in the previous video is an open cast on.
Here are some variations:
  • Open Cast on with a cast on Comb (shown in the video)
  • Open Cast on with a wire
  • Open Cast on with Ravel cord
Most knitters graduate beyond these methods pretty quickly.
The following cast on methods leave open stitches to be worked later. For example, leave open stitches, then pick them up and hand knit some ribbing. Or turn the knitting, pick up open stitches and knit reverse stockinette.
  • Scrap and Ravel
  • Using a Cast on Rag
You will use these again and again

Closed Cast on
With a closed cast on, the starting stitches are secure.
These techniques can be categorized:
  • Closed but temporary.
    These cast on methods are quick and have their place ... they just wouldn't be appropriate for the finished edge of your next sweater.
    Uses:
    • Cast on for swatching
    • Scrap 'n Ravel Cast on
    • Cut 'n Sew
  • Closed and Functional
    These techniques can be used for the edges of your knitting, without any additional finishing.
    • E-wrap cast on (lots of variations)
    • Chain Cast on

For with many more bind-off techniques, visit:
the Knit it Now Classroom: Bind off Methods

Almost magical, stitch patterning on this machine happens with a combination of the carriage settings, the punchcard and the memory drum.

Overview:

The settings for each stitch pattern are a little different, but the overall steps for creating a stitch pattern are as follows:
  1. Insert and lock the punchcard
  2. Carriage on the left and set for plain knitting
  3. Pass the carriage from left to right, memorizing the stitch pattern
  4. Carriage on the right
  5. Release the punchcard
  6. Set the carriage for the desired stitch pattern
  7. Continue knitting

blocks.title: About Automatic Patterning on this Machine

components.html:
We can knit so much more than plain stockinette with this machine. The punchcard mechanism can automatically create textured and multi-color stitch patterns.
It is critical that you understand the 3 elements that create stitch patterns.
3 settings control stitch patterning:
1
Needle position
2
Side Levers
3
Cam Lever

1
Needle position
Letters marked on the side of the needlebed A-B-C-D represent:
A Non-working position  (NWP)  Unused needles
B  Working Position (WP)  Needles lined up to knit in stockinette and most pattern work
C  Middle Position (MP)  Bring the needles from holding position into working and pattern work positions
D  Holding Position (HP/Hold)  The farthest position from "A" on the needlebed

2
Side Levers
The Side Levers direct the butts of the needles through the channels under the carriage. It instructs the machine that you are going to be knitting in pattern.
This setting COMBINED WITH the Cam Lever create stitch patterning on your machine.

3
Cam Buttons
The Cam Lever tells the machine which stitch type you want to knit. Along with the Side Levers, the Cam Lever controls the action of the needles for specific stitch types.
  Tuck
  Skip | Slip
Stockinette
  Thread Lace | Punch Lace
  Knit-In | Fairisle

For more about punchcards, visit:
the Knit it Now Classroom: Punchcards

The punchcard mechanism:

1
Punchcard snaps
These snaps hold the card in a circle so it can rotate and repeat the stitch pattern.
Be sure to lap the card so there is no interruption of the pattern and the card flows smoothly in the mechanism

2
Stop Knob
Allows the advancement of the punchcard either manually or with the carriage
Locks the rotation of the card

3
L Knob
The L Knob controls the advancement of the card
  • "S": The card advances 1 row at a time (Normal knitting)
  • "L": The card advances with 2 passes of the carriage (double high)
4
Card Feeding Dial
Use to manually advance the card

The default setting for the L Knob is "S". With this setting the punchcard will advance 1 row with each pass of the carriage.
By setting the L Knob to "L" you instruct the punchcard mechanism to expand the stitch pattern design to "double high".
Instead of the card advancing once for each pass of the carriage, the card advances once for every 2 passes of the carriage.
With this setting, this stitch pattern is distorted which can produce interesting results WITHOUT punching a new card.
This technique can be applied to other stitch pattern types, slip, weaving, etc. Care should be taken with tuck stitch, too many tucks can cause problems.

If you are using an asymmetric design, be aware of how you are inserting the card. The final orientation of the design will depend on how you are knitting your garment.
Considerations:
  • Top down or hem up knitting
  • Right Side or wrong side facing stitch patterns
Test the design and the orientation of the card before starting your garment.
Some of the original punchcards had A-B-C-D markings on the card. Pattern instructions may have read "Insert Card 9B". This insured that you inserted the card #9 with the letter B at the lower corner and your design would match the pattern.

You may have the original punchcards for your machine, but you also may have "inherited" other cards. Here is something to consider.
The different brands of machines have different punchcard mechanisms. Although many cards are interchangable, lining up the first row of knitting can be different for each machine.
When you insert the card, the first row of the design "disappears" into the punchcard opening. You need to establish where the first row of the stitch pattern is located inside the mechanism.
Once you determine the location for your machine, mark your own line on your card so there's no guessing the next time.

The 360 came with a set of punchcards and the manual refers to them by number.
  • Standard Punchcards
  • Lace Punchcards
  • "Ribber" cards
NOTE: The ribber does not select needles. "Ribber" cards are designed for Double Bed Jacquard

Here are 4 accessories that are needed for automatic patterning.
We will discuss them in detail in the associated techniques sections.

Yarn Separators

If your yarn tangles with the round brushes under the carriage, try using the Yarn Separators on each side. This is especially recommended when knitting Fairisle.

Point Cams

Used for single motif knitting, position left and right point cams to isolate a stitch pattern. For example, knit a single repeat of a stitch pattern in the middle of the knitting.
Pattern knitting only happens between 2 point cams.
  • When setting Point cams at both edges of the knitting, the pattern will be knitted across the entire row.
  • When knitting isolated motif, position the point cam on each side of where you want the motif to knit, keeping the other sections in plain knitting.

Edge Pins (lace carriage)

Used in conjunction with the Point Cams and Magic Cams the Edge Pins helps isolate the needle selection for Single Motif Lace.

Magic Cams

Used along with the Point Cams and Edge Pins (lace) the Magic Cams control the needle selection when knitting isolated motifs

End needle selection

Consideration needs to be give to the end needles when working in patten.
To keep the edge stitches tidy (and make seaming easier) be aware of the end needle instructions in each stitch pattern technique.
Manually putting the end needle(s) into "D" position forces the carriage to knit those stitches and not tuck, slip or mis-pattern along the edge.
If you are finding long floats or edge stitches aren't knitting properly, consider manually selecting the end needle according to the following:

Tuck 2 end needles to "D" on CARRIAGE SIDE
Fairisle End needle to "D" on CARRIAGE SIDE
Slip End needle to "D" OPPOSITE the CARRIAGE
Punch Lace End needle to "D" BOTH SIDES
Knit Weave 1 needles to "D" on CARRIAGE SIDE
Plaiting Not needed
Single Motif Not needed

For easier seaming and neater edges, prevent the end needles from patterning.
Having a tuck or slip stitch on the edge of the knitting distorts the edge.
Use this one little trick for neat edges.

Tuck is a great way
to add texture and interest to your knitting.
When knitting tuck, certain needles do not knit and the working yarn travels OVER the needles out of work.
Once you understand how tuck stitch is created on your machine, the sky's the limit!
  • Change the number of rows tucked
  • Change the needles selected
  • Change the number of rows between tucks
  • Put some needles out of work
  • Add color
  • Mix 'n match stitch patterns

The often over-looked technique of Knitweave creates beautiful knitted fabrics with lots of possibilities.
Unlike traditional weaving, think of weaving on the machine as "laying-in" a second yarn on top of the knitting.
It is a decorative technique that can be used to create interesting textures and incorporate yarn that may not be suitable for your machine.

Often overlooked, Thread Lace is an easy technique to create openwork "lace" fabrics.
It's not fairisle, it's not true lace, but it's a unique stitch pattern that can create beautiful knit fabrics.
Knit with a thick yarn and a very fine yarn, there are lots of possibilities with your machine
NOTE:
Thread lace is knitting is very similar to Fairisle knitting with 2 differences:
  1. Choose a stitch pattern with short floats (1-2 stitches) The yarn is carried behind the "lace" openings. If the floats are too long, the appearance of lace is lost

Do not attempt to use the lace carriage until you have mastered stitch patterning.

To create eyelet lace with transferred stitches, this machines uses a separate lace carriage. The lace carriage transfers stitches and knits a row in one pass of the carriage. It replaces the main bed carriage.
This is unlike Brother/Knit King machines that have separate carriages for transferring and knitting.
Setting up for lace knitting is similar to setting up for other stitch types using punchcards. Lace punchcards are unique, however.
Looking at the example punchcard, you'll notice that the holes are spaced differently than a card used for tuck.
  • Each hole represents a stitch transfer
  • Stitch tranfers happen individually (no 2 holes next to each other)
  • Stitch transfers occur with AT LEAST 1 row of plan knitting between

There are 2 styles of lace:
Plain Lace: Eyelets are formed and are transferred in one direction per row of knitting.
Fashion Lace: Multiple eyelets are formed with transfers happening with multiple passes of the carriage per row of knitting.

Threading the lace carriage

Unlike the main bed carriage, the Yarn Feeder on the lace carriage moves.
Ensure that you thread it correctly
  • Manually slide the Yarn Feeder to the left
  • Position the yarn so that it is completely engaged.

Unlike Plain Lace, Fashion Lace has stitches transferred in multiple directions on the same row of knitting.
Following the punchcard, the Lace Carriage Cam Lever is moved between and to control if the carriage is knitting or transferring stitches.

Fashion lace cards have indicators for the rows where only transfers are occurring:

  • Pass the carriage and transfer stitches for the indicated section only
  • Return the cam lever to

Fashion Lace is created with multiple passes of the lace carriage. Depending on the carriage setting (and the punchcard) some passes of the carriage will transfer stitches only and other passes of the carriage will transfer and knit.

Charting devices allow the knitter to follow a schematic for the shaping of their knitting. Instead of following written text instructions or a chart, follow the lines to know when to increase and decrease to shape your knitting.
This machine is unusual in that the Knit Contour is built into the machine instead of being a separate device.
With a charting device you can use the provided garment outlines or draw your own outlines of garment pieces at half scale. For example, use a sewing pattern and duplicate the shape (at half scale) on a Knit Contour Pattern Paper and duplicate the design with your machine.
As you knit, the machine advances the Pattern Paper and the drawing according to your row gauge. You follow the lines on a scale that represents your stitch gauge.
The secret to success with a charting device (and all knitting)
is accurately measuring and recording gauge.


For more about Swatching, visit:
the Knit it Now Classroom: Swatching is NOT Optional

4 steps:
1
Establish YOUR gauge
2
Set up the Row Gauge Scale
3
Select and insert Stitch Scale
4
Set the Paper Pattern

1
Establish YOUR gauge
Establish your gauge over 40 stitches and 60 rows

2
Once you establish YOUR row gauge (in 4"/10cm) use these dials to set the machine.
  1. Set the Change Dial to
    The Row Number Dial will turn freely
  2. Turn the row number dial until your ROW GAUGE is displayed in the Row Number Window
  3. Set the Change Dial
    If your row gauge is between 30-60:
    set the Change Dial to 30-60
    If your row gauge is between 61-120:
    set the Change Dial to 30-60
    This will instruct the device to advance the pattern paper accordingly

3
Select and Insert a Stitch Scale
The Stitch Scales are designed to represent different stitch gauges (4"/10cm) measured by the Gauge Scale (ruler) or with a regular ruler.
  1. Choose the scale for your stitch gauge
  2. Set the paper lever to (up)
  3. Insert the scale behind the clips
NOTE: Some scales have the zero in the center of the scale. These are used for garment pieces that are shaped on both sides, like slacks and leggings.
In general the scales with zero on the left are used and the shaping is mirrored as needed

4
Insert and set the Paper Pattern
  1. Set the paper lever to (down) to release it
  2. Slip the paper pattern into the slot
  3. Pull the paper through to align it (use the center lines on front and back)
  4. Set the paper lever to (up) to engage it.

  1. Use the Feeding Dial to position the paper

With the Knit Contour set up correctly, as the carriage moves back and forth, the pattern sheet advances giving us visual instructions for our knitting.
The lines on the sheet align with the stitch scale and indicate the needles in work. When the line on the sheet "moves", we will increase or decrease stitches, keeping the number of stitches on the needlebed equal to the numbers on the scale.

slides.caption:
The supplied knitting diagrams have multiple sizes on a page.
TIP: Use a highlighter to note your size and make it easier to follow
This line indicates that I should have 67 stitches in work on the right side of zero.

As the knitting progresses and the pattern sheet advances we follow the lines.

  • Row numbers on the left (follow your row counter)
  • For the armhole we would bind off 13 stitches according to the scale
Following the line, on this row, we'd decrease 1 stitch
At the neckline we would work decreases following the lines on both sides

components.html: As you are knitting, it is important that the carriage hits the Feed Lever. This feed lever controls both the Knit Leader advancement AND the row counter advancement.
